findings.title: Shutdown uses Queue APIs unavailable on supported Python versions
findings.body: `Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were only added in Python 3.13. On earlier supported interpreters, `q.shutdown()` raises `AttributeError` (which is merely logged here), leaving workers blocked indefinitely in `Queue.get()`. Each subsequent `join(timeout=5)` then waits its full timeout, so the default 20-worker consumer can spend roughly 100 seconds shutting down and leak daemon threads.

findings.title: The worker queues are unbounded, so a slow group can exhaust process memory
findings.body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to an unlimited size, while `submit` always accepts work immediately. A slow result or persistently slow group therefore causes its queue, retained `WorkItem` payloads, and offset-tracker sets to grow without bound while the Kafka consumer continues polling. This provides no natural backpressure despite the strategy's stated guarantee and can OOM the consumer during a backlog.

findings.title: Normal strategy close can abandon work and miss its final offset commit
findings.body: `close` stops and joins the commit thread before shutting down the workers. A worker that finishes its current item after the commit thread's final iteration will mark the offset complete with no thread left to commit it. In addition, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets every worker's shutdown flag before draining queued items, so workers exit after at most their current item. A normal rebalance/deploy can therefore leave completed work uncommitted and replay it after restart, producing duplicate result side effects rather than performing the advertised graceful shutdown.

findings.title: Negative max-workers silently acknowledges every message without processing it
findings.body: The CLI accepts any integer for `max_workers`, and a negative value is truthy here, so `FixedQueuePool` is constructed with a negative queue count. Its initialization creates no queues; each submission then raises while indexing `self.queues`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that exception and adds/completes the offset, allowing the commit loop to acknowledge messages that were never sent to a worker. Validate that the configured queue/worker count is positive instead of accepting negative values.

findings.title: Worker exceptions are acknowledged as successfully processed
findings.body: The `finally` block completes the offset even when `result_processor` raised and the exception was only logged by the preceding handler. Once earlier offsets complete, the commit loop will commit this failed message and Kafka will not retry it, permanently dropping failed result handling. This contradicts the strategy's documented promise to commit only after successful processing; failures need to remain outstanding or be routed through an explicit retry/DLQ policy.
